Adorn
uh-DORN
v.
Latin adornare: ad- (to) + ornare (to furnish, decorate)—the root of ornament and, further back, of order. To adorn is to set in order so as to make beautiful, not merely to cover.

Biblical Definition

To adorn is to make beautiful by ordering, and Scripture is neither embarrassed by beauty nor neutral about what is being displayed. Isaiah uses it of salvation itself in unashamedly festive terms: he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation... as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels (Isa 61:10). Beauty is not the problem. The apostolic instruction concerns proportion and direction. Paul writes that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array (1 Tim 2:9), and the following verse supplies the substitute—good works, which is what he actually wants them adorned with. Peter says the same with a jeweler's phrase: the true ornament is the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price (1 Pet 3:4). He does not say the visible is worthless; he says the imperishable is the valuable one. And Titus extends adorning past clothing altogether: bondservants, by honesty and fidelity in ordinary work, adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things (Titus 2:10). That is the widest use—a life can be the ornament that makes a doctrine look like what it is. The question Scripture asks of any adorning is simply what it is advertising.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines ADORN as to deck or decorate; to make beautiful; to add to beauty by dress or ornaments; and to display the beauty or excellence of a thing.

expand to see more

ADORN, v.t. — To deck or decorate; to make beautiful; to add to beauty by dress; to deck with external ornaments.

ADORN, v.t. — To set off to advantage; to add ornaments to; to embellish by any thing external or adventitious; to display the beauty or excellence of. That they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour (Titus 2:10).

Key Scripture

1 Timothy 2:9 — "In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;"

Titus 2:10 — "Not purloining, but shewing all good fidelity; that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things."

1 Peter 3:4 — "But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price."

Isaiah 61:10 — "I will greatly rejoice in the LORD, my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels."

Modern Corruption

Adorning has become total self-presentation—the body as the entire message, curated and published continuously—while Scripture asks what the ornament is advertising and answers with good works, a quiet spirit, and a doctrine made visible.

expand to see more

The platform age turned adorning into a full-time occupation with an audience attached. Appearance is no longer preparation for a life; it is the product. The apostolic correction is not a dress code but a redirection: Paul's not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls is followed immediately by what he does want on display—good works. Peter names the imperishable ornament, the meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price—a valuation deliberately stated in jeweler's terms against a market that prices the other thing.

The opposite corruption is a sourness that treats beauty as suspect and drabness as holiness. Isaiah blows that away: salvation itself is described as a bridegroom decking himself and a bride putting on her jewels, and the tabernacle was made for glory and for beauty. Scripture's issue is never that a woman is lovely or a room is beautiful; it is proportion and direction. Titus supplies the widest and most searching form—an honest worker who does not pilfer adorns the doctrine, which means a life can make the gospel look like what it actually is, or like something else.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kosmeō, to arrange, order, adorn—the root of cosmos and cosmetic; Hebrew adah, to deck oneself with ornaments.

expand to see more

Greek kosmeō (G2885) — to put in order, arrange, adorn; the same root as kosmos, the ordered world, so adorning is ordering into beauty (Matt 12:44; 1 Tim 2:9; Titus 2:10; Rev 21:2).

Greek kosmos (G2889) — order, ornament, and hence the world; used for adorning in 1 Pet 3:3, where the outward adorning is contrasted with the hidden man of the heart.

Hebrew adah (H5710) — to ornament, deck oneself; used of the bride adorning herself with jewels (Isa 61:10; Jer 4:30; Ezek 16:11).

Usage

"Adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour—an honest worker's life as the ornament."

"The ornament of a meek and quiet spirit—priced by God, in jeweler's language."

"Isaiah 61:10 — salvation described as a bride putting on her jewels. Beauty is not the problem."
